Frogmore is one of 4 watermills on the River Gade listed in the Domesday Book in 1086.  For the next 7 centuries the mill was used either for milling corn or for  'fulling' woollen fibres until, in 1774, it was converted to the making of paper which has been its role ever since. 

It was in 1803 that Frogmore entered the pantheon of industrial heritage sites when it was leased by  the Fourdrinier brothers for the purpose of developing the  world's first paper machine, built for them by Bryan Donkin to the design of Louis Nicholas Robert whose patent they had acquired and registered in England two year's previously. The inherent weaknesses of this first machine were rectified in 1804 when the much improved forerunner of what we now know as the Fourdrinier Paper Machine was installed and operated at Frogmore.

Today Frogmore houses 2 Fourdrinier machines and, whilst still making paper, is also a visitor attraction for guided tours and a wide variety of education and community uses.
